By recording and directly refuting their claims, divine speech invites every seeker to employ sound reason and spiritual discernment, discovering that eternal accountability is the only coherent foundation for human life.
verses.35:
> “There is nothing beyond our first death, and we will never be resurrected

**The Materialist Creed Articulated**

The core doctrine of pre-Islamic Arabian materialism is laid bare in its raw, uncompromising simplicity: *in hiya illā mawtatunā l-ūlā wa-mā naḥnu bi-munsharīn* — “There is nothing beyond our first death, and we will never be resurrected. The syntax employs a restrictive negative construction: *in* (functioning as *mā*, there is not) followed by the exceptive particle *illā* (except, beyond). They assert that human existence is bounded strictly by the biological event of physical death; once a person dies and their bones decompose into dust, the human story is permanently closed.

This assertion represents the definitive rejection of bodily resurrection (*al-baʿth*), judgment, and eternity. In the pagan imagination, the universe was governed not by a purposeful, all-wise Creator, but by the blind, inexorable churning of physical time (*ad-dahr*). As the Qur'an records their philosophy elsewhere: *“There is nothing but our worldly life! We die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time!”* (45:24). Verse 35 encapsulates this bleak, reductionist worldview: human life is a temporary biological accident, ending in absolute, irreversible annihilation.

**The Paradox of "Our First Death"**

Classical exegetes, including al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and al-Qurṭubī, explored the intriguing phrasing *our first death* (*mawtatunā l-ūlā*). If they believed that death was absolute and final, why did they qualify it as the *first*? Does not calling something *first* logically imply the possibility of a second?

The commentators explained that the pagans used *first death* to designate the only death they acknowledged—the physical termination of their worldly existence—in contrast to the dual cycle of death and life proclaimed by the Prophet ﷺ. The Qur'an taught that human beings experience two deaths and two lives: nonexistence prior to conception, followed by worldly birth, followed by physical death, followed by resurrection on the Day of Judgment (as articulated in 2:28 and 40:11: *“They will say, ‘Our Lord, You made us lifeless twice and gave us life twice’”*). The pagans mockingly rejected this theological framework, insisting: there is only the single, physical death we see with our eyes, and nothing beyond it.

**The Emphatic Denial of Resurrection**

The second clause reinforces their skepticism with absolute grammatical finality: *wa-mā naḥnu bi-munsharīn* — and we will never be resurrected. The nominal sentence introduced by the negative *mā*, reinforced by the independent personal pronoun *naḥnu* and the emphatic preposition *bāʾ* attached to the passive participle *munsharīn* (from *n-sh-r*), conveys total, unshakeable rejection. The root *n-sh-r* specifically denotes spreading out, unfolding, reviving dead vegetation through rain, and resurrecting decomposed bodies from the earth.

To the pagan mind, the idea that scattered, pulverized bones mixed with desert dust could ever be reconstituted, re-clothed with flesh, and re-animated with conscious souls was physically impossible and laughable. When the pagan chieftain Ubayy ibn Khalaf took a crumbling bone, pulverized it in his hands, and blew the powder into the face of the Prophet ﷺ, he sneered: *“Who will revive these bones when they are rotted?”* (36:78). Verse 35 documents this deep sensory skepticism, where human beings judge the limits of divine omnipotence strictly by their own finite, material experience.

**The Moral Consequences of Denying the Afterlife**

The denial of resurrection is not merely an abstract metaphysical error; it is a moral catastrophe that fundamentally corrupts human behavior. If there is no afterlife, no cosmic accountability, and no ultimate justice, then human morality loses its transcendent foundation. Right and wrong become subjective human constructs, and the pursuit of selfish pleasure, power, and wealth becomes the only rational objective in a brief, meaningless life.

This direct link between the denial of resurrection and moral decadence is visible throughout pre-Islamic society. Because the Quraysh believed that *there is nothing beyond our first death*, they felt completely free to exploit the weak, break treaties when advantageous, and indulge their physical appetites without restraint. The fear of standing before an impartial Judge was erased from their consciousness. The Qur'an targets their skepticism with relentless intensity precisely because resurrection is the indispensable cornerstone of all ethical responsibility.

**The Intellectual Arrogance of Sensory Empiricism**

The pagan argument recorded in verse 35 represents an early form of naive sensory empiricism. They argued: because we have never seen a dead person return from the grave, resurrection is impossible. They refused to acknowledge any reality that transcended immediate sensory observation, foolishly assuming that the boundaries of their personal vision were the boundaries of cosmic reality.

This intellectual arrogance ignored the obvious signs of divine creative power that surrounded them daily. The God who created the boundless expanse of the heavens, who brought human beings into existence out of utter nothingness from a drop of fluid, and who revives the dead, barren desert into lush greenery through descending rain, undeniably possesses the power to reconstruct human bodies a second time. Their skepticism was not a product of profound philosophical insight, but of an unimaginative intellect blinded by material familiarity.

**The Tragic Illusion of Escaping Accountability**

The assertion *we will never be resurrected* reveals a desperate, underlying psychological desire to escape consequences. Deep within their consciences, the oppressors knew that if a Day of Judgment truly existed, their record of tyranny, persecution, and exploitation would doom them to terrifying punishment. Denying the Resurrection was an existential defense mechanism: by convincing themselves that the grave was the final end, they sought to silence the haunting voice of accountability.

Verse 35 records their desperate wishful thinking with devastating clarity. They declared themselves exempt from resurrection, but their declarations altered nothing in the divine decree. The verse sets the stage for the subsequent divine refutations, which will demonstrate that the Day of Decision is an appointed, inescapable reality where every human soul will be resurrected to face the sovereign King of the universe.
